summary: Describes the Telnet encryption option, a generic method of providing data confidentiality for the Telnet data stream. Specific ciphers are defined in companion documents.

eli5.summary: Telnet sends text where anyone can read it. This adds a way to scramble it, and other documents choose the scrambler.

questions: what is the telnet encrypt option
subtitle: A generic Telnet option that lets either side scramble its half of the conversation, leaving the choice of cipher to companion documents.

tldr.problem: Telnet has no protection from a gateway or eavesdropper reading IP packets as they cross the network, which is especially dangerous when passwords travel as clear text.
tldr.mechanism: The ENCRYPT option (code 38) negotiates, per direction, which encryption type to use, exchanges any initial data, and then brackets encrypted data between START and END commands.
tldr.outcome: It protects against passive watching but not active attackers, and none of its mechanisms provide data integrity. The RFC points to TELNET START_TLS as the direction for future work.

today: RFC 2946 is a Proposed Standard (September 2000) and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC itself notes that its mechanisms lack data integrity and points to TELNET START_TLS for future work.

sections.title: Why Telnet Needs Encryption
sections.content:
The Telnet protocol has no form of protection from an intervening gateway looking at IP packets as they travel through the network. The RFC calls this especially dangerous when passwords are sent as clear text over the network.

The ENCRYPT option is a generic method of providing data confidentiality for the Telnet data stream. It does not define a specific encryption algorithm. Separate documents are to be published defining implementations of the option for each algorithm.
sections.eli5: Anyone standing along the road can read an open postcard. This option is a way to put the message in a locked box instead.

sections.title: Command Names and Codes
sections.content:
The option itself is ENCRYPT, option code 38. Its subnegotiation commands are IS (0), SUPPORT (1), REPLY (2), START (3), END (4), REQUEST-START (5), REQUEST-END (6), ENC_KEYID (7) and DEC_KEYID (8).

The RFC also lists encryption types: NULL (0), DES_CFB64 (1), DES_OFB64 (2), DES3_CFB64 (3), DES3_OFB64 (4), CAST5_40_CFB64 (8), CAST5_40_OFB64 (9), CAST128_CFB64 (10) and CAST128_OFB64 (11). Future type numbers are assigned by the IANA under a First Come First Served policy.
sections.eli5: Each kind of message and each kind of scrambler has its own number, like a menu where you order by number instead of by name.

sections.title: Who May Send What
sections.content:
The usual Telnet WILL, WONT, DO and DONT commands work as usual: WILL ENCRYPT says the sender is willing to send encrypted data, and DO ENCRYPT says it is willing to receive it. The option must be negotiated in both directions, and the default is WONT ENCRYPT and DONT ENCRYPT, meaning no encryption.

Each subnegotiation command is reserved for one side. Only the DO ENCRYPT side may send SUPPORT, REPLY, REQUEST-START, REQUEST-END and DEC_KEYID. Only the WILL ENCRYPT side may send IS, START, END and ENC_KEYID.

The receiver of SUPPORT lists encryption types in order of preference, most preferred first. If it supports none of them, it should send IS NULL to show there is nothing in common, and it may also send WONT ENCRYPT. If ENCRYPT is used together with AUTH, SUPPORT MUST NOT be sent until the session key has been determined.
sections.eli5: It is like a walkie-talkie with rules: one side asks what scramblers you know, the other picks one, and each side only says the lines that belong to its part.

sections.title: Starting and Stopping Encryption
sections.content:
Only the sender of WILL actually transmits encrypted data. It begins with IAC SB ENCRYPT START ... IAC SE, and encryption starts at the octet right after that command. It ends after IAC SB ENCRYPT END IAC SE. While it is on, all data in that direction, including Telnet options, is encrypted. If a second START arrives before an END, it is ignored. Receiving IAC WONT ENCRYPT while encrypted data is arriving counts as receiving END.

The DO side can ask the other side to begin with REQUEST-START or to stop with REQUEST-END.

A keyid says which key to use when several are known. It is variable length, at least one byte, sent most significant byte first, and zero is reserved for the default key, typically one derived during authentication. The only valid keyids for START are those received in a DEC_KEYID command. ENC_KEYID and DEC_KEYID let the two sides check that a keyid maps to a valid key, and omitting the keyid means no common keyid was found.
sections.eli5: Encryption is like putting on a secret-language hat: a START message says the hat is on, and an END message says it is off again.

sections.title: A Worked Exchange
sections.content:
The RFC's example has Host1 ask Host2 to encrypt what Host2 sends. Host1 sends DO ENCRYPT, Host2 answers WILL ENCRYPT, and Host1 sends REQUEST-START and a SUPPORT list naming DES_CFB64.

Host2 then sends IS DES_CFB64 CFB64_IV with the initial feed, and Host1 acknowledges with REPLY DES_CFB64 CFB64_IV_OK. Because a REQUEST-START was received, Host2 sends START and everything it sends is encrypted until it sends END, after which data is clear text again.

The RFC expects any implementation that supports the ENCRYPT option to support all of this specification.
sections.eli5: One computer asks for a secret code, the other agrees and sends a starting puzzle piece, the first one confirms, and then the secret talking begins.

sections.title: Security Limits
sections.content:
Used alone, ENCRYPT protects against passive attacks, such as someone watching IP packets pass by, but not against active ones. An attacker who can modify packets in flight could prevent the option from being negotiated. Using the Telnet Authentication option (RFC 2941) alongside it fixes this: setting ENCRYPT_USING_TELOPT in the authentication-type-pair can force encryption to be negotiated even under active attack.

An active attacker can also interfere with starting or restarting encryption. If the user requested encryption and the client cannot enable or re-enable it, the client MUST assume it is under attack and immediately terminate the connection.
sections.eli5: The lock keeps out people who only look, but a sneaky person who can change messages might stop the lock from being used, so you also need to check who you are talking to.

sections.title: Future Directions
sections.content:
None of the encryption mechanisms under this option provide data integrity. The RFC says this is because of the complexity of specifying a protocol that provides integrity efficiently in a stream-oriented protocol.

The TELNET START_TLS specification gives confidentiality, integrity and compression, and the RFC says future work on Telnet encryption should examine it closely. One promising approach it describes is the anonymous Diffie-Hellman mode of TLS, followed by the Telnet AUTHENTICATION option with an authentication mechanism that includes the client and server finished messages from the TLS negotiation.
sections.eli5: The locked box hides the message but cannot tell you if someone scribbled on it. A newer idea would add that check too.

messages.label: DO ENCRYPT
messages.note: Host1 asks Host2 to negotiate encryption of the data Host2 sends.

messages.label: REQUEST-START
messages.note: Enable encryption as soon as initialization is complete.

messages.label: REPLY DES_CFB64 CFB64_IV_OK
messages.note: Host1 acknowledges receipt of the IV.

messages.label: START
messages.note: All data from Host2 to Host1 is now encrypted.

items.label: IS
items.desc: WILL side states the encryption type and initial data.

items.label: SUPPORT
items.desc: DO side lists the types it supports, most preferred first.

items.label: REPLY
items.desc: DO side continues the initial data exchange.

items.label: END
items.desc: Following data will not be encrypted.

items.label: REQUEST-START
items.desc: DO side asks the remote side to begin encrypting.

items.label: REQUEST-END
items.desc: DO side asks the remote side to stop encrypting.

items.label: ENC_KEYID
items.desc: WILL side asks the other side to verify a keyid.

items.label: DEC_KEYID
items.desc: DO side asks the other side to verify a keyid.
